Below is a (non-exhaustive) catalogue of the most-cited families of methods that have been applied to **knowledge-graph (KG) tasks** such as link-prediction / KG completion, entity classification, relation extraction, KG-enhanced question answering, and KG-based recommendation.  For each family I give a short description, the canonical papers (with year and venue), and a few representative follow-up works that extend or combine the idea.

---

## 1. Translational Embedding Models  
*Idea:*  Model a relation **r** as a translation vector that moves a head entity **h** toward a tail entity **t** (or a more complex geometric operation).  

| Model | Core Paper | Key Features / Extensions |
|-------|------------|---------------------------|
| **TransE** | Bordes *et al.* 2013, *NIPS* | Simple - ‖h + r − t‖₂ scoring. Works well for 1-to-1 relations. |
| **TransH** | Wang *et al.* 2014, *AAAI* | Projects entities onto relation-specific hyperplanes before translation (handles many-to-many). |
| **TransR / CTransR** | Lin *et al.* 2015, *AAAI* | Embeds entities and relations in separate spaces; uses a projection matrix per relation. |
| **TransD** | Ji *et al.* 2015, *AAAI* | Dynamically generates projection matrices from entity and relation embeddings (fewer parameters). |
| **TransSparse** | Gu *et al.* 2020, *ICLR* | Sparse relation-specific projection matrices for very large KGs. |
| **RotatE** | Sun *et al.* 2019, *ICLR* | Interprets relations as rotations in complex space (still a translational-style scoring). |
| **HAKE** | Xiao *et al.* 2020, *ICLR* | Decomposes each relation into a “hierarchy” (modulus) and “orientation” (phase) component. |

**Why they matter:**  Translational models were the first that scaled to millions of triples and remain strong baselines for link-prediction benchmarks such as FB15k-237, WN18RR, YAGO3-10, and Open-KGs (e.g., Wikidata5M).

---

## 2. Semantic-Matching (Bilinear / Tensor) Models  
*Idea:*  Score a triple by a similarity (dot-product, bilinear, or tensor) between transformed embeddings of **h**, **r**, and **t**.

| Model | Core Paper | Highlights |
|-------|------------|------------|
| **RESCAL** | Nickel *et al.* 2011, *ICML* | Full relation-specific matrix; expressive but O(d²) parameters per relation. |
| **DistMult** | Yang *et al.* 2015, *ICLR* | Diagonal relation matrix → simple dot-product; works well for symmetric relations. |
| **ComplEx** | Trouillon *et al.* 2016, *ICLR* | Extends DistMult to complex numbers; can model antisymmetric relations. |

**Fault diagnosis** (also called fault detection, isolation, and identification - FDI) is a mature research area that spans many engineering domains (manufacturing, aerospace, power systems, process control, robotics, etc.).  Over the past three decades a large toolbox of analytical, statistical, and data-driven techniques has been developed.  Below is a non-exhaustive but representative catalogue of the most-used methods, grouped by the underlying paradigm, together with key references (papers, books, or seminal authors) that introduced or popularized each approach.

---

## 1. Model-Based (Analytical) Methods  

| Method | Core Idea | Typical Applications | Representative References |
|--------|-----------|----------------------|----------------------------|
| **Parity-space / Observer-based residual generation** | Build a mathematical model (state-space, transfer function).  Residuals are generated by comparing measured outputs with model predictions (e.g., Luenberger observer, Kalman filter).  Faults are detected when residuals exceed thresholds. | Aerospace systems, industrial process plants, motor drives. | *Patton, G. (1999). “Generalized observer-based fault detection.”*; *Isermann, A. (2006). “Fault-diagnosis systems: An introduction from fault detection to fault tolerance.”* |
| **Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) / Unscented KF (UKF) based diagnosis** | Non-linear state estimation; the filter’s innovation sequence is used as a residual. | Robotics, UAV navigation, chemical reactors. | *Grewal, M. & Andrews, A. (2001). “Kalman Filtering Theory and Practice.”* |
| **Sliding-mode observers** | Robust to bounded uncertainties; generate residuals that are insensitive to disturbances. | Power converters, motor drives. | *Edwards, C., & Spurgeon, S. (1998). “Sliding Mode Control: Theory and Applications.”* |
| **Parameter estimation / Adaptive observers** | Identify changes in model parameters (e.g., stiffness, resistance) that indicate a fault. | Gearbox health monitoring, hydraulic systems. | *Liu, Y., & Wang, J. (2008). “Adaptive observer based fault detection for nonlinear systems.”* |
| **Analytical Redundancy Relations (ARRs)** | Derive algebraic equations that must hold for a healthy system; violations signal faults. | Chemical process plants, aircraft engines. | *Venkatasubramanian, V., et al. (2003). “A review of process fault detection and diagnosis.”* |
| **Bond-graph / Energy-based modeling** | Use physical-law based bond-graph models to generate residuals that respect energy conservation. | Mechanical systems, mechatronics. | *Gawronski, W. (1990). “Bond Graphs: Modeling, Analysis and Simulation.”* |
